name: Toscana IGT

climate: Rain picks up at harvest. Growers race to pick before rot sets in, and vintages vary more.

soil.rock: Limestone makes alkaline soil that drains well yet can hold water for the vines. It is usually planted to grapes valued for their acidity. Shale and mudstone are fine-grained rocks that hold heat well and are moderately fertile.

land: The high ground runs about 7°F cooler than the low ground. Higher vineyards ripen later and keep more acidity, so one grape can make lighter or richer wine here depending on height.

winkler: Early and mid-season grapes make good wine.

sheet.place: Toscana IGT covers the whole region and leaves winemakers free to choose their grapes. Many Super Tuscans use it because their blends did not fit the old Chianti rules.

claims.claim: Toscana IGT (now IGP) is a regional designation. Its production zone is the whole of Tuscany, with about 13,300 to 13,500 hectares of vines in use.

Law 164 of 1992 introduced the IGT category in Italy. It sits between the strict DOC and DOCG and the plain vino da tavola. The Toscana IGT disciplinare was issued by ministerial decree on 9 October 1995 (Gazzetta Ufficiale 25 October 1995).
Blended Toscana IGT wines may use any proportions of the grape varieties approved for Tuscany. A wine that names one variety on the label must be at least 85% of that variety.

Types listed are bianco, rosato, rosso and novello, white and rose sparkling (metodo classico or tank), late harvest, and white and red passito. Minimum alcohol is listed as 10.0% for bianco, 11.0% for rosato, rosso and novello.
The designation is large. The Consorzio Vino Toscana says over 4,000 producers, an average of about 640,000 hl declared a year and about 27% of Tuscany's wine output.

Consorzio Vino Toscana is recognised by the Ministry (Masaf) as the protection body for all Toscana IGT producers. It was formed on 10 June 2019. Its earlier forms were the Ente Tutela Vini dei Colli della Toscana Centrale (founded 22 November 1984 by Piero Antinori, Vittorio Frescobaldi and Ambrogio Folonari) and from 27 July 1995 the Ente Tutela Vini di Toscana.

A revised disciplinare drops the old form Toscano o Toscana, leaving Toscana, and adds sparkling wine categories. Reports say the national wine committee approved it in March 2026 and EU approval is still to come.

Chianti DOC (1967) set a recipe of 50 to 80% Sangiovese, 10 to 30% Canaiolo, 10 to 30% Trebbiano and/or Malvasia (white grapes) and up to 5% others. This blocked Sangiovese-Cabernet blends and 100% Sangiovese from using the Chianti name.

Sassicaia (Tenuta San Guido, Bolgheri) was the first. Mario Incisa della Rocchetta planted Cabernet Sauvignon in 1944. The first commercial wine was the 1968 vintage, released in 1971. It was sold as vino da tavola because the blend fell outside DOC rules.

Tignanello (Antinori, Chianti Classico area) first reached the market with the 1971 vintage. It was sold as vino da tavola because it broke Chianti Classico norms, which required white grapes in the blend. Giacomo Tachis worked on it with Piero Antinori. Cabernet was added in 1975.
The first Tignanello of 1971 was Sangiovese with a small share of Canaiolo, aged 30 months in barriques. The current blend is 85% Sangiovese, 10% Cabernet Sauvignon and 5% Cabernet Franc.
Montevertine's 100% Sangiovese Le Pergole Torte was refused by the Chianti authorities and released as vino da tavola in 1977.

Sassicaia, Tignanello and other early Super Tuscans were sold as vino da tavola, the bottom rung. From 1992 the new IGT category gave them a rung with a regional name. WSET says Super Tuscans became the home of the IGT category from 1992. Later some moved into DOCs such as Bolgheri.
Under the 1992 law, vino da tavola could no longer show a vintage or a grape name, so producers moved to IGT to keep both on the label.

Super Tuscan is an unofficial term, not recognised in the Italian classification. It describes Tuscan reds, often with Cabernet or Merlot, made outside the old DOC rules. Some are IGT Toscana, some are DOC (such as Bolgheri) and Sassicaia has its own DOC.
Bolgheri DOC dates from 1983 and the Sassicaia subzone from 1994. Some sources wrongly give 1994 for the whole DOC.
Chianti Classico DOCG covers a delimited zone, defined by a 1932 decree and based on the old 1716 Chianti boundaries. Toscana IGT covers the whole region.

Chianti Classico DOCG needs 80 to 100% Sangiovese for annata and Riserva, plus red grapes suited to Tuscany for the rest. No white grapes are listed. Gran Selezione needs 90 to 100% Sangiovese, with the rest limited to listed native reds (Colorino, Canaiolo, Ciliegiolo, Mammolo, Pugnitello, Malvasia Nera, Foglia Tonda, Sanforte) up to 10%.
White grapes were allowed in Chianti Classico until 2006. The 2006 vintage was the first without them. 100% Sangiovese was allowed from 1996, when Chianti Classico became its own DOCG.

Chianti Classico vineyards must be on hills, no higher than 700 m, on soils mostly of sandstone, calcareous marl, clay schist, sand and gravel. Toscana IGT has no such restriction shown in the sources I read.

Chianti Classico rules: annata wine is sold from 1 October of the year after the harvest. Riserva needs at least 24 months of aging, Gran Selezione at least 30, both with at least 3 months in bottle, counted from 1 January after the harvest.
Chianti Classico DOC came in 1967 and DOCG in 1984. The Gran Selezione level was added in the 2013 reorganisation, dated 2014.
